Short Description: A seventeen-book geographical work combining regional description, history, ethnography, mythology, and discussion of earlier geographical writers. Strabo draws on authors such as Homer, Eratosthenes, Herodotus, and Polybius as well as travel and personal observation. The work surveys the inhabited world from Iberia and the Atlantic to India and is an important source for the geography and political landscape of the early Roman Empire.

Short Description: A concise anatomical treatise devoted to the Greek names of the parts of the human body. Moving systematically through the body, Rufus records anatomical terminology and observations while distinguishing ordinary usage from more technical medical vocabulary. The work is especially valuable for the history of Greek anatomical nomenclature and medical education.

Name: On the Interrogation of the Patient
Metaphysical Tags: Phenomenology (Experiential), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: A short medical treatise on the physician’s questioning of the patient. Rufus argues that diagnosis requires information that observation alone cannot supply, including the patient’s symptoms, habits, previous illnesses, and individual experience of disease. It is the only surviving ancient medical work devoted specifically to dialogue between physician and patient.

Name: On Melancholy
Metaphysical Tags: Phenomenology (Experiential), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: A medical monograph on melancholia, now reconstructed from Greek, Latin, and especially Arabic fragments rather than preserved complete. Rufus relates melancholic conditions to black bile and discusses different manifestations, including fear, sadness, disturbed thought, and forms associated with digestive or hypochondriac complaints. The work became highly influential in later Greek, Arabic, and medieval medical traditions.

Name: Synopsis on the Pulse
Metaphysical Tags: Phenomenology (Experiential), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: A compact Greek treatise on pulse theory traditionally attributed to Rufus of Ephesus. It discusses the origin and character of the pulse and summarizes distinctions used in ancient sphygmology. Modern scholarship treats the attribution to Rufus as uncertain, so the work is best used as evidence for pre-Galenic or early imperial pulse theory rather than as securely Rufian doctrine.

Short Description: A monumental public inscription commissioned by Diogenes, a wealthy Epicurean of Oenoanda in Lycia. Carved across a wall roughly 80 meters long, it presented Epicurean ethics, physics, epistemology, theology, maxims, letters, and reflections on old age in a civic setting. Diogenes explains that he wished to make Epicurean teaching publicly available as a remedy for fear and false belief, especially fear of death and the gods.

Short Description: A large corpus of speeches, declamations, hymnic prose, polemics, and public addresses associated with the Second Sophistic. Individual works include praise of Rome, Athens, Smyrna, and other cities, historical declamations, defenses of rhetoric, and addresses to gods and imperial authorities. The corpus displays Aristides’ commitment to classical Greek paideia while also revealing the ways a provincial Greek intellectual negotiated life within the Roman imperial order.

Name: Sacred Tales
Metaphysical Tags: Phenomenology (Experiential), Becoming (Process Ontology), Monism (Single Principle), Apophatic–Aporetic (Unknowable)
Short Description: A six-book autobiographical work centered on Aristides’ long illnesses, dreams, and devotion to Asclepius. It records divine instructions concerning baths, diet, travel, sacrifice, exercise, and other therapies, while also using the language and forms of contemporary medical case history. Rather than simply opposing sacred healing to medicine, the work shows religious experience and Greco-Roman medical culture interacting within Aristides’ account of suffering and recovery.

Name: Orphic Hymns
Metaphysical Tags: Apophatic–Aporetic (Unknowable), Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Monism (Single Principle), Phenomenology (Experiential), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Subversion (Negation)
Short Description: A collection of eighty-seven Greek hymns composed for ritual use by an Orphic or Dionysiac religious community in Roman-period Asia Minor, probably in the second or third century CE and perhaps around the middle of the third century. Each hymn invokes a deity or cosmic power through epithets and commonly specifies an offering or fumigation before requesting favor, peace, health, or protection. The collection preserves a distinctive Roman-period form of Orphic ritual poetry while drawing on much older Greek mythic and religious traditions.

Name: Oneirocritica (Interpretation of Dreams)
Metaphysical Tags: Phenomenology (Experiential), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Becoming (Process Ontology), Apophatic–Aporetic (Unknowable)
Short Description: A five-book treatise on dream interpretation by the professional diviner Artemidorus. The first three books present general principles and extensive classes of dream symbols, while Books IV–V were written more directly for his son and discuss practice, interpretation, and collected cases. Artemidorus repeatedly emphasizes the dreamer’s occupation, social position, sex, circumstances, and local custom, presenting oneiromancy as a disciplined interpretive craft informed by travel, earlier writings, and accumulated experience.

Name: On Epideictic Speeches
Arts and Sciences Tags: Education, Public Relations, Literature, Art / Aesthetics, Philosophy
Short Description: A late-third-century rhetorical handbook transmitted under the name of Menander Rhetor. It gives detailed guidance for epideictic and ceremonial speeches, including addresses to emperors and officials, civic encomia, wedding speeches, funeral orations, invitations, leave-takings, and festival speeches. The two surviving epideictic treatises transmitted under Menander’s name are generally thought not to be by the same author, and this second treatise may therefore be the work of another late antique rhetorician.

Short Description: A four-book medical compendium addressed to Oribasius’ friend Eunapius and designed for a non-specialist reader with some medical knowledge. It condenses material from the larger Medical Collections into practical guidance on hygiene, diet, simple drugs, diseases, and readily available treatments. The work belongs to Oribasius’ broader project of preserving and reorganizing earlier Greek medicine, especially Galenic material, in accessible handbook form.

Metaphysical Tags: Phenomenology (Experiential), Becoming (Process Ontology), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: A vast medical compilation produced at the request of Emperor Julian. Originally comprising about seventy books, it excerpts and organizes material from earlier Greek medical authors, especially Galen but also many writers whose works are otherwise lost. Only part of the collection survives complete. Its chief historical importance lies in Oribasius’ systematic preservation and arrangement of earlier medical knowledge rather than in the introduction of a new medical system.

Short Description: A large corpus of speeches and rhetorical works ranging from autobiography and imperial panegyric to civic advocacy, educational concerns, and defenses of traditional cult. Libanius presents classical Greek paideia and rhetoric as essential elements of civic life while addressing the political and religious transformations of the fourth-century Roman Empire. Some orations, especially For the Temples, explicitly defend traditional religious institutions, but the corpus as a whole is broader than pagan apologetic.

Short Description: A vast surviving correspondence of more than 1,500 letters written across Libanius’ long career. The letters address students, teachers, officials, friends, governors, and emperors and illuminate education, patronage, illness, civic petitions, appointments, personal relationships, and religious tensions in the fourth-century eastern Roman Empire. They are especially valuable for reconstructing the social and administrative networks linking Antioch with the wider Greek-speaking imperial world.

Short Description: A corpus conventionally numbered as forty-five orations, though one is widely regarded as spurious. The authentic speeches include theological discourses, funeral orations, festal sermons, autobiographical and apologetic addresses, and the famous Theological Orations delivered at Constantinople in defense of Nicene Trinitarian theology. Gregory combines classical rhetorical training with Christian preaching and doctrinal argument across works composed in Cappadocia and Constantinople.

Short Description: A large and varied body of Christian Greek poetry using classical meters and literary forms. Gregory writes on theology, Scripture, moral instruction, friendship, illness, ecclesiastical conflict, mortality, and his own life, with important autobiographical poems reflecting on his career and withdrawal from public office. The corpus shows classical Greek poetic culture being deliberately adapted to Christian doctrine, self-reflection, and religious instruction.
